facts: A **prism** has **two identical, parallel bases** and the same shape all the way through (uniform cross-section).
A **pyramid** has **one base** and its side faces are triangles that meet at a single point, the **apex**.
Prism side faces are **rectangles**; pyramid side faces are **triangles**.
Slice a prism parallel to its base and every slice is the same shape; a pyramid's slices shrink towards the apex.
steps: Count the bases: two matching ends → prism; one base → pyramid.
Look for an apex (a single top point): yes → pyramid.
Check the side faces: rectangles → prism; triangles → pyramid.

foundation.solution_text: It is a prism because it has two identical, parallel bases.
It is a pyramid because its triangular side faces meet at one apex.

foundation.question_text:
A solid has the same triangular cross-section all the way through.
Is it a prism or a pyramid?
foundation.solution_text: The cross-section is uniform, so the solid is a prism.

foundation.question_text:
A solid has one hexagonal base and six triangular faces meeting at one point.
Is it a prism or a pyramid?
foundation.solution_text: It has one base and an apex, so it is a pyramid.
The prism has two identical parallel bases; the pyramid has one base.

foundation.question_text: What happens to slices parallel to the base as you move through a prism?
foundation.solution_text: Every slice stays the same shape and size because the prism has a uniform cross-section.

development.question_text: Mia says, “Every solid with triangular faces is a pyramid.” Explain why she is not correct.
development.solution_text: A triangular prism has two triangular bases and rectangular side faces, so a solid can have triangular faces and still be a prism.
Its orientation does not change its properties: it has two matching triangular bases and is a prism.

development.question_text:
A solid has two congruent pentagonal faces joined by five rectangles.
State two properties that identify it.
development.solution_text: It has two identical parallel bases and a uniform pentagonal cross-section, so it is a prism.

development.question_text:
A square-based solid is sliced parallel to its base.
The slices become smaller towards the top.
What type of solid is it?
development.solution_text: Shrinking parallel slices show that the solid tapers to an apex, so it is a pyramid.
Both have pentagonal bases. The prism has two bases and a uniform cross-section; the pyramid has one base and an apex.

development.question_text:
A builder makes a solid with one rectangular base and four triangular side faces.
Does it have a uniform cross-section?
Explain.
development.solution_text: No. It is a rectangular pyramid, so parallel slices shrink as they approach the apex.

mastery.question_text:
A hidden solid has no apex.
Every slice parallel to one end is a congruent trapezium.
Classify the solid and justify your answer.
mastery.solution_text: It is a trapezoidal prism because the cross-section is uniform and there is no apex.

mastery.question_text:
Two solids both have a square face.
Explain why that fact alone cannot tell whether either solid is a prism or a pyramid.
mastery.solution_text: The square could be one of two matching bases of a prism or the single base of a square pyramid; the other faces and any apex must be checked.

mastery.question_text:
A solid has six vertices and five faces.
Could it be a triangular prism or a square pyramid?
Explain.
mastery.solution_text: It could be a triangular prism: it has two triangular bases and three rectangular faces. A square pyramid has only five vertices.
